To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
myeloma cells do not "home" to the bone marrow, but rather are induced to proliferate there because of growth factors expressed by normal bone-marrow cells.

constitutive expression of cytokines by normal bone marrow stromal cells may be responsible for the preferential expansion of myeloma cells in the bone marrow, and that the induction of cytokine expression by myelomas in other organs may account for the progression of myeloma from a localized to a systemic disease.

(1) myeloma cells express IL-6 receptors, but do not home to bone marrow; (2) myeloma proliferation is dependent on IL-6-like growth factors; and (3) myeloma induces expression of growth factors in spleen cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of growth factors in the pathogenesis of myeloma, a disease of plasma cells.
the pathophysiology of multiple myelomas.
the mechanisms by which myeloma cells home to bone marrow and proliferate there.
